title: Democratic Rep. Jimmy Gomez resigns after damning House ethics report | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

Democratic Rep. Jimmy Gomez is resigning from Congress on the heels of a damning report from the House Ethics Committee that found he “made sexual contact” with a congressional aide without her consent.

The ethics panel concluded that “Representative Gomez’s conduct caused this House staffer significant and ongoing distress and contributed to her decision to leave House employment altogether.”

Within an hour of the panel making its findings public, the California congressman issued a statement announcing his resignation effective December 1.

“I have strong disagreements with the Committee’s report and its conclusions. Among other significant deficiencies and omissions, the report does not include key portions of my testimony that are essential to a full and fair understanding of what occurred. I also have serious concerns about the process. In my interview, I answered the Committee’s questions only to see my statements selectively quoted, disparaged, and disregarded throughout the final report, to which I was given no opportunity to respond,” he said.

“With this in mind, I see no other alternative than to resign, effective December 1, to allow for my staff to close out important constituent casework and needs.”

Gomez was not set to return to Congress in January after having lost reelection to his Los Angeles-area seat earlier this month. But his departure in the final days of the current Congress comes as the House has reckoned repeatedly this year with bombshell allegations of sexual harassment against members of both parties. Gomez is the third member to resign this year in the face of sexual misconduct allegations.

The ethics panel made the Gomez report public as part of atranche of investigative findingsreleased Monday.

The culmination of a months-long probe, the report found that “Representative Gomez failed in his obligation to behave in a manner that reflects creditably on the House, and his conduct was exacerbated by his failure to appreciate the inherent power imbalance between House Members and House staff.”

It does not name the woman, who “repeatedly referenced a toxic and predatory culture” on Capitol Hill and alleged Gomez made sexual contact with her without her consent in 2024, according to the report. CNNpreviously reportedthat the former staffer, who was in her mid-twenties and worked for a House leadership office at the time of the incidents, had spoken with the committee.

The women’s attorneys told CNN in a statement that the panel’s report “confirms that Representative Gomez sexually harassed and assaulted our client while she was a staffer on Capitol Hill.”

“Representative Gomez abused the power given to him by the voters when he violated this young woman, effectively destroying her dreams of a career in public Service,” attorneys Lisa J. Banks and Sarah E. Nesbitt said.

According to the report, the woman, identified as “Witness 1,” told the investigative panel that Gomez had sexually assaulted her at a bar in Washington, DC, and later groped her in his office.

CNN has independently spoken with the woman and individuals close to her, as well as reviewed text messages that corroborate what she told the ethics panel.

The woman told CNN that she first met Gomez at a birthday party in February 2024, and that they later met with acquaintances at a downtown bar. There, the woman said, Gomez told her that he had noticed her around the US Capitol.

The woman told lawmakers that she asked Gomez when men start focusing on how good women are at their jobs, rather than how they look. “Usually when a woman turns 40 is when they get respect,” she recalled him saying.

Gomez, according to the woman, “put his hand down [her] skirt and then put his fingers inside of [her].” Describing the incident as “nonconsensual whatsoever,” she recalled that she “probably flinched” and “was shocked by it.” She ultimately ran to the bathroom, where she began to cry, according to the report.

Later, the woman said she allowed Gomez to kiss her outside of the bar because she hoped that it would help her to leave the situation.

Gomez claimed the exchange was consensual in his testimony to the committee.

In another encounter that summer, the woman said Gomez grabbed her and tried to kiss her in his office before she told him “no” and left the room.

CNN has also spoken with the woman’s friend about the toll it took on her physical and mental health after she left Washington following that second incident. According to this person, she seemed “distraught and depressed” and started losing hair.

The woman’s attorneys said their client “sacrificed her own sense of safety and privacy to help reveal the ongoing misogyny and debauchery that permeates Capitol Hill” and called for Congress to take “immediate steps” to rein in that culture.

“Democracy cannot function properly when women must endure harassment and abuse as a condition of public service,” they said.

Recent high-profileallegations of sexual assault and harassmentagainst lawmakers in both parties have brought renewed scrutiny to how Capitol Hill handles the issue and members of Congress hold those within their own ranks accountable.

Last week, the House Ethics Committee took steps to speed up probes into sexual misconduct, including changing how the bipartisan panel issues subpoenas and codifying its policy of publicly disclosing findings when lawmakers’ behavior violated House rules.

Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to serve as House speaker, along with Katherine Clark and Pete Aguilar, who will serve in Democratic leadership, called Gomez’s resignation “appropriate.”

“The report of wrongdoing and abuse of power by Rep. Gomez is serious and deeply troubling. It is appropriate that he is stepping down. Decisive action to set a new standard for reform is an urgent priority for House Democrats,” they said in a joint statement.

Investigators on Monday also made public reports alleging that retiring Rep. Troy Nehls violated campaign finance rules and may have accepted impermissible contributions, and that outgoing Rep. Mike Collins’ former chief-of-staff improperly hired and paid his then-girlfriend around $10,000 for 16 weeks of pay as an intern.

CNN has reached out to Gomez, Nehls and Collins for comment.

The committee found that Collins’ former chief-of-staff had an “improper employment relationship” – dating a woman the office hired to be an intern. Collins, the committee said, did not exercise “sufficient oversight” of his staffer.

The panel ultimately came to an agreement with Collins that his office would pay $2,880 back to the US Treasury, noting that the Georgia Republican cooperated with their investigation. But the panel asserted his former chief, Brandon Phillips, “evaded subpoena service on numerous occasions, including three attempts by the U.S. Marshals Service,” and ultimately voted to hold Phillips in contempt.

“The Committee found that Representative Collins’ congressional office had an improper employment relationship with Witness 1, impermissibly paying her $10,000 as an ‘intern’ for 16 weeks on the payroll in 2023 and 2024, while accepting voluntary communications services from her over several years,” the panel said in their report, though they noted that they “did not find evidence that Representative Collins was directly involved in the hiring of Witness 1 or the use of her services for official purposes.”

CNN has attempted to reach out to Phillips for comment.

Collins is leaving Congress in January; he challenged Democrat Sen. Jon Ossoff for his Senate seat and lost earlier this month.

The committee also asserted that Nehls improperly handled campaign funds when he used a company he owns, Liberty 1776 LLC, as a political committee to take in and disburse funds for his campaign. The committee noted that his violations were “the result of inattention to the applicable standards of conduct” rather than “knowing and willful.”

“Representative Nehls’ missteps were far from the most egregious campaign finance violations before the Committee in recent years, and Representative Nehls himself is no longer campaigning for Congress,” the committee wrote.

“Nonetheless, the public’s trust in the integrity of its legislators is inextricably linked to legislators’ adherence to the campaign finance requirements governing them. Representative Nehls did not take those requirements seriously enough, nor did he take the Committee’s role in reviewing this matter seriously enough; the Committee must make clear more is expected of House Members,” the committee wrote.

Nehls did not run for reelection this year, but his twin brother, Trever Nehls, won the race to replace him next Congress. The committee wrote that its report would serve as a formal reprimand of the congressman’s actions, and that the matter is now considered closed.

This headline and story have been updated with additional developments.
